newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti suspended after new CEO named.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti suspended after new CEO named.

text.p: The stock of Italy's money-losing Olivetti was suspended on the Milan bourse Thursday just as it rebounded after the appointment of new Chief Executive Roberto Colaninno.

The appointment late Wednesday of Colaninno, a close ally of former Chairman Carlo De Benedetti, punctuates two weeks of crisis at the information technology group, which has seen its finances come under market scrutiny and its stock plunge to record lows.
Traders warned that the sharp rise in the share price Thursday was more a reflection of short-term speculation on the volatile stock than a vote of confidence in the new chief executive.
"There's no point in rushing to buy now. The situation still isn't clear and the new man is considered a De Benedetti clone," said a broker in Milan.
"We have no new information to suggest it's a turnaround situation just yet and the way the stock has been moving recently, it's more like going to a casino."

The stock fell to a record low of 465 lire at the start of the week and has repeatedly hit automatic suspension tripwires since. It first sank to the bottom of a 10 percent trading limit and then ran up against the ceiling on Thursday before the bourse officially opened for trade.

The shares closed Wednesday at 510 lire ahead of the emergency board meeting in which the chief executive of three months, Francesco Caio, was ousted and replaced by Colaninno, head of auto components group Sogefi.
Colaninno's appointment was the latest twist in events since De Benedetti resigned from the Olivetti board on Sept. 3 after 18 years as chairman, apparently losing a power battle with Caio.

But De Benedetti, who remains Olivetti's largest shareholder with a 15 percent stake, is reported to have been the prime mover behind the ousting of Caio, his former assistant who masterminded the launch last year of Olivetti's 41.3 percent owned Omnitel mobile phone venture.

Analysts speculate Colaninno may be a stop-gap figure who will run Olivetti while it hunts for a prominent figure in the telecommunications industry to push it forward in the phone sector, widely viewed as its best hope for future survival.
Colaninno is widely seen as enjoying the confidence of De Benedetti, and the former chairman's industrial holding company CIR also controls Sogefi, founded by Colaninno in 1981.
But analysts and traders were wary about hailing Caio's departure and Colaninno's arrival as a turnaround, warning that problems highlighted in the last two weeks have not gone away.
The company side-stepped key questions about its business put by market regulators by issuing a statement early Wednesday giving details of some of its affairs but leaving out others.

Caio, current chairman Antonio Tesone and De Benedetti are being investigated by magistrates in Olivetti's home town of Ivrea in northwest Italy who suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its financial position, judicial sources say.
